1111.event_title: Robert Burns writes A Red, Red Rose
1111.event: In 1794 the Scottish poet Robert Burns produced the song now known as A Red, Red Rose. It compares the speaker's love to a red rose newly sprung in June and to a sweetly played melody, and goes on to promise that his love will last until the seas run dry. It became one of the best-known love lyrics in English and Scots.
1111.explanation: The song shows how naturally poets in very different cultures reach for the freshest flower they know as the measure of the person they love.
1111.tie_back: The kural praises the delicate anicham flower and then says the beloved is more delicate still; Burns likewise reaches for the finest flower he knows, a rose just opened in June, as the measure of his love.
1111._accuracy_note: Comparing the beloved with a perfect flower fits, but Burns makes the two alike, while the kural's point is that she surpasses even the most delicate flower.

1112.event_title: Shakespeare's Sonnet 130 rejects the usual comparisons
1112.event: Shakespeare's sonnets were first printed in 1609 in a quarto published by Thomas Thorpe. Sonnet 130 begins by saying that the poet's mistress's eyes are nothing like the sun, and goes on to deny that her lips are coral red or her cheeks like roses. In its closing couplet the poet says his love is as rare as any woman who has been praised with false comparisons.
1112.explanation: The sonnet is famous for poking fun at the stock flattery of love poetry while still declaring real love.
1112.tie_back: The kural scolds the lover's heart for imagining that common flowers anyone can see resemble his beloved's eyes, and Sonnet 130 likewise refuses the stock comparisons for a mistress's eyes, insisting that she is beyond such ordinary likenesses.
1112._accuracy_note: Both reject the standard comparison for the beloved's eyes, though Shakespeare does it with teasing realism while the kural does it to raise her above any comparison.

1113.event_title: Kalidasa's Meghaduta describes the yaksha's beloved
1113.event: The Sanskrit poet Kalidasa, writing in about the fifth century CE, composed the Meghaduta (The Cloud Messenger), a lyric love poem of some 115 verses. In it an exiled yaksha, a nature spirit, asks a monsoon cloud to carry a message to his beloved in the Himalayan city of Alaka, and much of the poem describes the landscapes along the cloud's route. In its second part the yaksha describes his very beautiful wife and her lonely state at home.
1113.explanation: The Meghaduta is one of the most admired poems of classical India, and it shaped how later Indian poets wrote about longing and beauty.
1113.tie_back: The kural paints the beloved's beauty through images taken from nature, and the Meghaduta likewise carries its reader through the natural world before arriving at a lover's description of his wife's beauty.
1113._accuracy_note: Next-best only: both portray the beloved's beauty in the language of nature, but the sources checked confirm only that the yaksha describes his wife, not the feature-by-feature comparisons that make this kural distinctive.

1114.event_title: The bust of Nefertiti is found at Amarna
1114.place: Amarna, Egypt; now in the Neues Museum, Berlin, Germany
1114.event: On 6 December 1912 a German excavation led by the archaeologist Ludwig Borchardt found a painted limestone bust of Queen Nefertiti in the ruins of the workshop of the court sculptor Thutmose at Amarna, Egypt. The bust is about 3,300 years old, and Nefertiti's name is usually translated as the beautiful one has come. Borchardt wrote in his diary of the find's liveliness, and the bust is now displayed in the Neues Museum in Berlin.
1114.explanation: The bust became one of the most famous images of beauty from the ancient world.
1114.tie_back: The kural imagines that the blue water-lilies, if they could see the beloved's eyes, would hang their heads in defeat; Nefertiti's face is a real-world case of beauty that, more than three thousand years later, still makes admirers feel that nothing else compares.
1114._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the event shows celebrated beauty, but it has nothing of the kural's playful picture of flowers ashamed before a beloved's eyes.

1115.event_title: Anna Pavlova first dances The Dying Swan
1115.event: The choreographer Michel Fokine created the short solo The Dying Swan for the Russian ballerina Anna Pavlova, set to Le Cygne from Camille Saint-Saëns's Carnival of the Animals. The dance portrays the last moments of a fragile, wounded swan. It became the role for which Pavlova is best remembered, and she performed it throughout her career.
1115.explanation: The solo became one of the most famous images in ballet of beauty so delicate that it seems about to break.
1115.tie_back: The kural jokes that the beloved's waist is so slender that the weight of a few flower stalks could break it and bring out the mourning drums; Pavlova's swan made that idea of breakable delicacy into a famous work of art.
1115._accuracy_note: Next-best only: just the idea of exquisite, breakable delicacy links them; the kural is playful hyperbole about a beloved, and the ballet is not about love.

1116.event_title: Chinese astronomers record the guest star of 1054
1116.event: On 4 July 1054 astronomers of the Song dynasty in China recorded the sudden appearance of a new star, which they called a guest star, near the star now known as Zeta Tauri. It was bright enough to be seen in daylight for about 23 days and remained visible at night for nearly two years. Modern astronomers identify it as the supernova whose remains form the Crab Nebula.
1116.explanation: The Chinese records are among the most important observations in the history of astronomy, linking an ancient sighting to an object still studied today.
1116.tie_back: The kural imagines the stars thrown into confusion because a second moon, the beloved's face, has appeared among them; the guest star of 1054 is a real occasion when a strange new brilliance appeared and disturbed the familiar order of the sky.
1116._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the image of a new light upsetting the heavens matches, but the event has no connection with love or with a beloved's face.

1117.event_title: Galileo shows that the Moon is not flawless
1117.event: From late November to mid-December 1609 Galileo Galilei observed and sketched the Moon through his telescope. In Sidereus Nuncius (The Starry Messenger), printed in Venice in March 1610, he reported that the Moon's surface was not smooth and perfect, as followers of Aristotle had taught, but rough and uneven, with dark markings, mountains and hollows.
1117.explanation: Galileo's observation helped overturn the old belief that the heavens were perfect and unchanging.
1117.tie_back: The kural asks whether the beloved's face carries any blemish like the dark spots on the bright moon; Galileo's telescope showed that the moon really is marked and uneven, the very flaw the poet says her face does not share.
1117._accuracy_note: The event confirms the moon's blemishes that the kural contrasts with the beloved's face, but it illustrates only the moon half of the comparison.

1118.event_title: Beethoven dedicates the Moonlight Sonata to Giulietta Guicciardi
1118.event: In 1801 Ludwig van Beethoven completed his Piano Sonata in C-sharp minor, Op. 27 No. 2, which was published in Vienna in 1802 with a dedication to the young Countess Giulietta Guicciardi, who had studied with him. Beethoven was deeply drawn to her and described her to friends as a lovely, enchanting girl. The name Moonlight Sonata was given only in the 1830s, when the poet Ludwig Rellstab compared its first movement to a boat on Lake Lucerne in moonlight.
1118.explanation: The sonata became one of the most famous piano pieces ever written, and its best-known name joins the moon to a work first offered to a young woman Beethoven admired.
1118.tie_back: The kural blesses the moon and tells it that it could win the poet's love only by shining like the beloved's face; in Beethoven's sonata the moon arrived only later as a nickname, while the music itself was given to the woman he admired.
1118._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the moon and a beloved meet in this famous work, but by later accident of naming rather than by any comparison of her face with the moon.

1119.event_title: Elizabeth Barrett Browning's private Sonnets from the Portuguese
1119.event: During her courtship with the poet Robert Browning, around 1845 and 1846, Elizabeth Barrett wrote a sequence of 44 love sonnets that she had not intended to publish. Robert later persuaded her of their worth, and they appeared in her Poems of 1850. She called them Sonnets from the Portuguese, suggesting they were translations, to protect the privacy of such personal poems; the title probably came from Robert's pet name for her.
1119.explanation: The sequence became one of the best-loved collections of love poetry in English, yet it began as words meant for one reader only.
1119.tie_back: The kural tells the moon that to resemble the beloved's face it must not show itself for everyone to see, because her face is for one viewer alone; Barrett's sonnets were likewise written for one reader, and even when published they were disguised as translations.
1119._accuracy_note: The idea of love kept for one person's eyes fits, though the kural concerns the beloved's face being seen, not poems being shared.

1120.event_title: Hans Christian Andersen publishes The Princess and the Pea
1120.event: On 8 May 1835 the Danish writer Hans Christian Andersen published The Princess and the Pea in his first collection of Fairy Tales Told for Children. In the tale an old queen tests a young woman who claims to be a real princess by placing a single pea under twenty mattresses and twenty eiderdown feather beds. In the morning the woman says she slept badly because something hard bruised her, and this extreme sensitivity proves she is a true princess.
1120.explanation: The tale became one of the best-known fairy tales in the world and a byword for extraordinary delicacy.
1120.tie_back: The kural says that even the soft anicham flower and swan's down feel like thorny burrs to the beloved's tender feet, and Andersen's princess, bruised by a single pea through forty layers of bedding, is the most famous storybook version of the same playful exaggeration.
1120._accuracy_note: The hyperbole of delicacy is almost identical, but the event is the publication of a fairy tale rather than a lover's real experience, and it is not a love scene.
